endorsements.title: Considerations for the regulation of generative AI-enabled medical devices (discussion paper)
endorsements.quote: This element considers whether intended users can actually understand the device’s outputs, their limitations, and when escalation is needed across varied health literacy levels; the avoidance of coercive, emotionally manipulative, or otherwise inappropriate or abusive language; and the risk of automation bias, in which a user accepts an output without appropriate scrutiny because of the device’s fluency or perceived authority.

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: It is also valuable to have a process for measuring user satisfaction – both with the AI solution and with the clarity of the information provided to them.

endorsements.quote: This can be 1601 accomplished by determining how and when information is needed, integrating contextually 1602 appropriate risk controls into the design of the product, and finally validating that the intended 1603 users receive and can functionally understand the key information in relevant use contexts.

endorsements.quote: These evaluation procedures must systematically incorporate feedback from individuals across the socioeconomic spectrum, educational continuum, and age distribution to identify potential interaction barriers that might otherwise remain undetected in homogeneous testing environments, thus preventing the inadvertent creation of technological solutions that exacerbate rather than ameliorate healthcare access disparities [ 4 , 19 ].

endorsements.title: A Clinician-Centered Evaluation Framework for Large Language Models in Patient Education: Integrating the Technology Acceptance Model and Medical Condition Regard Scale
endorsements.quote: We recognize that the primary limitation of the framework is that the PEOU scores are currently designed to be provided by clinician proxies rather than by patients themselves.

evidence.title: Comparing ChatGPT-4 and Human Translation of an Outcome Questionnaire: A Randomized, Double-Blinded Non-inferiority Study
evidence.outcome: Patient-rated comprehension before and after patient face validation and questionnaire revision
evidence.effect: ChatGPT-4 understandability increased from 4 (2–5) to 5 (3–5); human medians remained 5. Between-translation p-values were 0.004 before and 0.082 after face validation. Results were not stratified by literacy.
evidence.quote: While the human-translated questionnaire initially performed better in terms of readability, comprehension, and appropriate use of language, the differences between the two versions disappeared following face validation.

evidence.title: Evaluating a retrieval-augmented pregnancy chatbot: a comprehensibility-accuracy-readability study of the DIAN AI assistant
evidence.outcome: Women's vs clinicians' Likert ratings of comprehensibility, accuracy, readability of chatbot responses
evidence.effect: Differences concentrated in postpartum care: comprehensibility favored women (p=0.012), accuracy favored women (p=0.018), readability favored clinicians (p=0.008); other domains showed no significant differences after correction.
evidence.quote: Other domains showed no significant between-group differences after correction.
evidence.sample_unit: evaluators (119 women, 29 clinicians) rating chatbot responses

evidence.title: Key Information Influencing Patient Decision-Making About AI in Health Care: Survey Experiment Study
evidence.outcome: Patient comprehension of AI label prototypes and information elements' effect on understanding
evidence.effect: 86.7% found labels easy to read, 84.2% easy to understand; information elements had no significant effect on legibility, comprehensibility, or overload.
evidence.quote: Most participants reported that the AI labels were easy to read (perceived legibility; 86.7%) and understand (comprehensibility; 84.2%).

evidence.title: The Illusion of Understanding: A Randomized Controlled Trial of LLM-Generated Lay Summaries of Brain MRI Reports
evidence.outcome: objective patient comprehension of reports with lay summaries
evidence.effect: 58.3% intervention vs 59.4% control (OR 0.97, P = .54); normal reports comprehension reduced (72.5% vs 76.6%, P = .001)
evidence.quote: LLM-generated lay summaries appended to brain MRI reports improved patient satisfaction and subjective comprehension but did not improve objective comprehension, indicating a gap between perceived and actual understanding that should be addressed before clinical integration.

evidence.title: Accuracy, readability, and understandability of large language models for prostate cancer information to the public
evidence.outcome: Lay user comprehension of simplified ChatGPT summaries via multiple-choice question
evidence.effect: MTurk workers (n=514) rated summaries clear (89.5-95.7%) but correctly understood content in 63.0-87.4%; scenario 1 only 63.0%.
evidence.quote: 449 (87.4%) MTurk workers correctly understood the content of the layperson summary of scenario 2 whereas only 324 (63.0%) correctly understood the content of the layperson summary of scenario 1.
evidence.sample_unit: prostate cancer questions (ChatGPT responses rated by 53 urologists/residents and 514 MTurk workers)

evidence.title: Multidimensional evaluation of large language models in radiology report readability
evidence.outcome: Comprehension of LLM-simplified reports by age and education level
evidence.effect: Significant age × education interaction on subjective and objective comprehension (P<0.05); lower education associated with lower comprehension
evidence.quote: The results of the second-stage 2 × 2 factorial analysis (age × educational level) demonstrated that age and educational level had significant interactive effects on both subjective and objective comprehension scores ( P < 0.05).
evidence.sample_unit: radiology reports (plus 800 patients in clinical setting validation)

commentary.bottom_line: Three simulated studies with 20 to 340 participants suggest that testing AI outputs with intended users can surface comprehension problems that clinician proxies and self-rated clarity may miss, but none stratified results by health literacy or measured escalation. Certainty that the practice prevents misunderstanding or missed escalation is very low.

perspectives.view: Three level 4 studies tested user comprehension, all in offline or simulated settings, with 20 to 340 participants. None stratified results by health literacy, and none measured whether users knew when to escalate. The designs, sample sizes, and indirect outcomes lead to a very low certainty rating that comprehension testing across literacy levels reduces misunderstanding.

In one hazard study, 89.5% to 95.7% of lay raters called summaries clear, yet 63.0% to 87.4% answered comprehension questions correctly. A French trial of 2,727 participants found lay summaries did not raise comprehension (58.3% vs 59.4%). Self-rated ease, as used in the 340-patient label study, may therefore overstate understanding, and objective checks may catch more errors.

In the UK study, 119 women and 29 clinicians rated the same chatbot responses differently in postpartum care. Comprehensibility favored women (p=0.012) and readability favored clinicians (p=0.008). In Denmark, revising a questionnaire after face validation with 20 patients raised ChatGPT-4 understandability from 4 to 5. Both findings suggest clinician proxies may not substitute for intended users.

A Chinese study of 320 reports found an age by education interaction on comprehension of simplified reports, and lower education was linked to lower comprehension (P<0.05). The practice tests included non-English speakers in Denmark and a racial and ethnic minority focus in the United States. None reported results by literacy or enrolled Medicaid or safety-net patients.

FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software asks developers to validate that intended users can functionally understand key information. NIST AI 600-1 calls for verifying user instructions through user testing, and a regulatory discussion paper names health literacy and escalation explicitly. The supplied studies do not show whether meeting these expectations changes patient outcomes.

No supplied study asked patients whether they knew when to contact a clinician or how to reach one after reading an AI output. In the French trial, comprehension of normal reports was lower with lay summaries (72.5% vs 76.6%, P = .001). This result suggests patients may misread results without anyone detecting the error.

commentary.research_gap: No study compared tested and untested AI outputs on downstream errors or escalation behavior. No study stratified comprehension by measured health literacy, and none was conducted in live deployment. Future work should use objective comprehension and escalation measures, enroll users across literacy levels, and report results by subgroup.
commentary.underserved_note: One practice test included non-English-speaking patients (Denmark, n=20), and one focused on racial and ethnic minority patients (United States, n=340). No test enrolled Medicaid or safety-net populations, and none stratified by literacy. A hazard study found lower comprehension among less-educated and older users, so it remains unknown whether comprehension testing detects failures in the groups most likely to experience them.
